To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) an achievable rate per bit per unit energy is derived for the multiple relay network, where transmissions take place over orthogonal channels; (2) the derived energy per bit is the minimum achievable energy per bit for this network.
a distributed energy allocation algorithm for a multiple relay network is derived.

a) a distributed implementation for a regenerative relaying scenario can be achieved by using a simple routing and power allocation algorithm and b) the achievable rate per unit power is a function of the number of relays, the source and relay powers, and the relay locations.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a multiple relay network where the source and destination are connected via multiple hops of regenerative relays.
the problem of energy efficiency in wireless networks, where we focus on the case where a single source transmits a message to a destination through the help of multiple relays.
the design of a distributed multiple relay system that maximizes the rate per unit energy.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the achievable rate per unit power is given by the minimum of the following three expressions: (a) the rate of the direct transmission between the source and the destination, (b) the sum of the rate of the source to relay link, and the relay to destination link, and (c) the rate of a single relay to destination link.
the presented results are useful to the design of energy efficient wireless networks.
the presented solution provides a distributed implementation that achieves a rate per unit energy of the network.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the achievable rate per unit total energy is given as follows: R= min (R1, R2), where R1 and R2 are the achievable rates for the two-hop relay networks with and without relays, respectively.
the proposed solution is a distributed one, and that the rate per unit energy achieved by the solution is within a multiplicative gap of 3 from the capacity of the network.
the achievable rate per unit power of the multiple relay network is the same as the one of the multiple access channel with a common message.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the energy per bit per hop (EPB) can be made arbitrarily small, while the rate per unit energy can be kept constant.
the achievable rate per unit of energy is not affected by the number of relays.
, in the absence of a global knowledge of the network, the optimal solution can be implemented in a distributed manner.
